clinicalPearls: A tiny intestinal fluke acquired by eating raw, salted or undercooked brackish-water and freshwater fish, common in the Nile delta, the Middle East and East Asia
Most infections are mild, but heavy burdens cause colicky abdominal pain, mucous diarrhoea and a sense of abdominal discomfort
Adult flukes lodge between the villi of the small intestine, producing shallow mucosal inflammation and superficial erosions
As with Metagonimus, eggs can occasionally embolise to the heart or central nervous system and produce serious ectopic granulomatous disease
Diagnosis is by finding small operculated eggs in stool that are almost indistinguishable from those of Metagonimus and the liver flukes
Praziquantel is the drug of choice and gives high cure rates
Prevention relies on avoiding raw or improperly preserved fish and on adequate sanitation
reference.pathophysiology: Heterophyes heterophyes is a minute heterophyid trematode whose life cycle involves brackish-water snails and euryhaline fish that harbour infective metacercariae. Humans acquire infection by consuming raw, salted or lightly cooked fish. Excysted larvae mature into small adult flukes that nestle deep among the villi of the small intestine, provoking localised mucosal inflammation, villous atrophy and superficial ulceration, which in heavy infection contributes to diarrhoea and mild malabsorption. Eggs deposited in the mucosa can occasionally penetrate lymphatics or vessels and embolise to distant sites such as the myocardium, spinal cord or brain, where they excite granulomatous reactions with potentially grave consequences. Eggs passed in faeces perpetuate the cycle by contaminating water.
additionalDifferentials: Metagonimiasis and other heterophyid intestinal fluke infection
Fasciolopsiasis and other intestinal trematode disease
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites with concentration methods
Repeated stool sampling because of low and intermittent egg output
Detailed egg morphometry to separate from other small trematode eggs
Cardiac or neurological imaging only when ectopic disease is suspected
redFlags: Cardiac symptoms or signs suggesting myocardial egg deposition
Neurological deficits raising concern for cerebral or spinal involvement
Persistent diarrhoea with weight loss indicating heavy infection
Lack of response to therapy prompting diagnostic review
reference.prognosis: Intestinal heterophyiasis has an excellent prognosis and clears rapidly with anthelmintic treatment; the uncommon cardiac or neurological ectopic forms carry a far more guarded outlook.
pitfalls: Confusing the eggs with those of opisthorchiid liver flukes owing to close morphological similarity
Missing light infections on a single stool examination
Dismissing non-specific gastrointestinal complaints as functional in endemic areas
Neglecting the possibility of egg embolisation when unexplained cardiac or neurological features arise
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Praziquantel is the anthelmintic of choice and achieves high cure rates for intestinal infection
Provide supportive care with oral rehydration and symptomatic relief of colicky abdominal pain and mucous diarrhoea
Prevent infection and reinfection by avoiding raw, salted or undercooked brackish-water and freshwater fish and by improving food-preparation hygiene
Confirm cure with follow-up stool examination, using repeated concentrated samples because egg output is low and intermittent
Manage the rare ectopic cardiac or neurological disease from embolised eggs with targeted imaging, specialist input and anti-inflammatory adjuncts
Escalate urgently if cardiac or central nervous system involvement is suspected, as the ectopic forms carry a far more guarded outlook
